quests.conceptTitle: Information Snap-In: Possessive Relative Pronoun whose
quests.questionSentence: The professor whose research grant was recently renewed will supervise three graduate students this year. What does 'whose' link together here?
quests.targetClause: The professor and the research grant, showing possession
quests.completedSentence: The professor whose research grant was recently renewed will supervise three graduate students this year. What does 'whose' link together here?
quests.ruleExplanation: 'Whose' links 'the professor' (the owner) to 'research grant' (the thing owned); the graduate students play no part in this possessive relationship.
quests.nativeTip: Remember that 'whose' always connects an owner to the noun sitting right after it.
quests.legoPreview: 🧩 Snap Slot: [defining] ➔ "The professor and the research grant, showing possession"

quests.conceptTitle: Information Snap-In: Omission of Object Relative Pronoun
quests.questionSentence: The internship ___ she applied for last spring finally responded with an offer.
quests.targetClause: (no word needed)
quests.completedSentence: The internship (no word needed) she applied for last spring finally responded with an offer.
quests.ruleExplanation: 'She' is the subject of 'applied for,' making 'the internship' the object; since it's a thing in a defining clause, the pronoun can be dropped entirely.
quests.nativeTip: 'She' already has a job in this clause - 'applied for.' Does this defining clause about a thing allow the pronoun to disappear?
quests.legoPreview: 🧩 Snap Slot: [defining] ➔ "(no word needed)"

quests.conceptTitle: Information Snap-In: Whom in Formal Register
quests.questionSentence: Which sentence is most appropriate for a formal scholarship application?
quests.targetClause: The mentor whom I worked with during my research project encouraged me to apply.
quests.completedSentence: Which sentence is most appropriate for a formal scholarship application?
quests.ruleExplanation: 'Whom' is the formally correct object pronoun for a person in this register; the other options are grammatical but progressively more casual or incorrectly punctuated for this context.
quests.nativeTip: Formal written applications favor the traditional object pronoun for a person over casual alternatives.
quests.legoPreview: 🧩 Snap Slot: [defining] ➔ "The mentor whom I worked with during my research project encouraged me to apply."

quests.conceptTitle: Information Snap-In: Defining vs Non-Defining Relative Clause
quests.questionSentence: The airline app, which crashed during check-in, has since been updated. Is this clause defining or non-defining, and why?
quests.targetClause: Non-defining - 'the airline app' is already a specific, singular thing, so the crash detail is extra information.
quests.completedSentence: The airline app, which crashed during check-in, has since been updated. Is this clause defining or non-defining, and why?
quests.ruleExplanation: 'The airline app' already refers to one specific app, so 'which crashed during check-in' is extra, non-defining detail, correctly set off with commas.
quests.nativeTip: Think about how many airline apps this sentence could be referring to - one specific one, or several needing narrowing down.
quests.legoPreview: 🧩 Snap Slot: [non-defining] ➔ "Non-defining - 'the airline app' is already a specific, singular thing, so the crash detail is extra information."

quests.conceptTitle: Information Snap-In: Reduced Passive Relative Clause
quests.questionSentence: Which is the correctly reduced form of 'Travelers who were delayed by the storm were rebooked on later flights'?
quests.targetClause: Travelers delayed by the storm were rebooked on later flights.
quests.completedSentence: Which is the correctly reduced form of 'Travelers who were delayed by the storm were rebooked on later flights'?
quests.ruleExplanation: 'Delayed' correctly reduces 'who were delayed,' dropping the pronoun and the auxiliary 'were,' and keeping the passive sense - the storm delayed the travelers.
quests.nativeTip: Drop 'who were' and keep only the participle that matches the passive meaning.
quests.legoPreview: 🧩 Snap Slot: [defining] ➔ "Travelers delayed by the storm were rebooked on later flights."

quests.conceptTitle: Information Snap-In: Relative Adverb of Place (where)
quests.questionSentence: The terminal ___ our connecting flight departs is a fifteen-minute walk from here.
quests.targetClause: where
quests.completedSentence: The terminal where our connecting flight departs is a fifteen-minute walk from here.
quests.ruleExplanation: 'Where' correctly shows that the terminal is the location of the departure, standing in for 'from which our connecting flight departs.'
quests.nativeTip: 'Departs' doesn't take a direct object here - the terminal is simply where the departing happens.
quests.legoPreview: 🧩 Snap Slot: [defining] ➔ "where"

quests.conceptTitle: Information Snap-In: Object Relative Clause with whom
quests.questionSentence: The specialist whom my doctor referred me to finally has an opening next week. Why is 'whom' correct here?
quests.targetClause: Because 'the specialist' is the object of 'referred' - 'my doctor' is the subject.
quests.completedSentence: The specialist whom my doctor referred me to finally has an opening next week. Why is 'whom' correct here?
quests.ruleExplanation: 'My doctor' is the subject of 'referred,' making 'the specialist' the object - which calls for 'whom.'
quests.nativeTip: Check who is doing the referring, and who is being referred.
quests.legoPreview: 🧩 Snap Slot: [defining] ➔ "Because 'the specialist' is the object of 'referred' - 'my doctor' is the subject."

quests.conceptTitle: Information Snap-In: Non-Defining Clauses Cannot Omit Their Pronoun
quests.grammarRule: Non-Defining Clauses Cannot Omit Their Pronoun
quests.questionSentence: My best friend, ___ I've known since childhood, is getting married next month.
quests.targetClause: whom
quests.completedSentence: My best friend, whom I've known since childhood, is getting married next month.
quests.ruleExplanation: Because this is a non-defining clause, signaled by the commas since 'my best friend' is already unique, the pronoun cannot be omitted and 'that' cannot be used; 'whom' is the formally correct choice for a person here.
quests.nativeTip: Notice the commas around this clause - does that change whether this pronoun, even though it's an object relative, could ever be dropped?
quests.legoPreview: 🧩 Snap Slot: [non-defining] ➔ "whom"

quests.conceptTitle: Information Snap-In: Omission of Object Relative Pronoun
quests.questionSentence: Which sentence would sound most natural in a casual social media caption?
quests.targetClause: This is the friend I met on my trip to Portugal!
quests.completedSentence: Which sentence would sound most natural in a casual social media caption?
quests.ruleExplanation: 'This is the friend I met on my trip to Portugal!' is the shortest, most natural phrasing for a casual caption, dropping the object relative pronoun entirely.
quests.nativeTip: Captions are short and casual - which option drops the unnecessary connecting word?
quests.legoPreview: 🧩 Snap Slot: [defining] ➔ "This is the friend I met on my trip to Portugal!"

quests.conceptTitle: Information Snap-In: Defining vs Non-Defining Relative Clause
quests.questionSentence: Fix this line from a resignation letter: 'I am grateful for the opportunities, that this company, has provided me.'
quests.targetClause: I am grateful for the opportunities that this company has provided me.
quests.completedSentence: Fix this line from a resignation letter: 'I am grateful for the opportunities, that this company, has provided me.'
quests.ruleExplanation: Since there could be many kinds of opportunities, this clause is defining and needs no commas at all; 'that' works fine once the commas are removed.
quests.nativeTip: Two things need fixing here: a pronoun that cannot follow a comma, and commas that don't belong in a defining clause at all.
quests.legoPreview: 🧩 Snap Slot: [defining] ➔ "I am grateful for the opportunities that this company has provided me."

quests.conceptTitle: Information Snap-In: Whom in Formal Register
quests.questionSentence: Which sentence is most appropriate for a formal cover letter?
quests.targetClause: The hiring manager whom I spoke with at the career fair mentioned this role.
quests.completedSentence: Which sentence is most appropriate for a formal cover letter?
quests.ruleExplanation: 'Whom' is the formally correct object pronoun for a person in this register; the other options are grammatical but progressively more casual, or add a comma that isn't clearly justified on a first mention.
quests.nativeTip: A cover letter is a formal document - check which object pronoun for a person matches that elevated register.
quests.legoPreview: 🧩 Snap Slot: [defining] ➔ "The hiring manager whom I spoke with at the career fair mentioned this role."

quests.conceptTitle: Information Snap-In: That Cannot Introduce Non-Defining Clauses
quests.questionSentence: Find the error in this professional email sentence: 'Please find attached the report, that summarizes our Q3 performance.'
quests.targetClause: 'That' should be 'which,' since it follows a comma.
quests.completedSentence: Find the error in this professional email sentence: 'Please find attached the report, that summarizes our Q3 performance.'
quests.ruleExplanation: 'That' can never follow a comma; since the report is already specifically identified as attached, 'which' is the correct fix.
quests.nativeTip: Identify the relative pronoun that is never allowed to follow a comma.
quests.legoPreview: 🧩 Snap Slot: [non-defining] ➔ "'That' should be 'which,' since it follows a comma."

quests.conceptTitle: Information Snap-In: Omission of Object Relative Pronoun
quests.questionSentence: Compare: A) 'The clause the lawyers debated for hours was removed.' B) 'The clause that the lawyers debated for hours was removed.' Which register is each suited to?
quests.targetClause: A is more casual (pronoun omitted); B is more neutral/formal (pronoun retained).
quests.completedSentence: Compare: A) 'The clause the lawyers debated for hours was removed.' B) 'The clause that the lawyers debated for hours was removed.' Which register is each suited to?
quests.ruleExplanation: Sentence A drops the object relative pronoun, giving it a slightly more casual feel; sentence B restores 'that,' which reads as more neutral or formal written English. Both are equally grammatical.
quests.nativeTip: Ask which version drops the pronoun, and which restores it in full.
quests.legoPreview: 🧩 Snap Slot: [defining] ➔ "A is more casual (pronoun omitted); B is more neutral/formal (pronoun retained)."

quests.conceptTitle: Information Snap-In: Omission of Object Relative Pronoun
quests.questionSentence: Which version belongs in a formal quarterly report rather than a casual conversation?
quests.targetClause: The metrics that the team tracked improved significantly.
quests.completedSentence: Which version belongs in a formal quarterly report rather than a casual conversation?
quests.ruleExplanation: 'The metrics that the team tracked improved significantly' keeps the pronoun and uses neutral, professional vocabulary throughout, unlike the increasingly casual alternatives.
quests.nativeTip: Formal reports spell out every grammatical element and avoid slang or sentence fragments.
quests.legoPreview: 🧩 Snap Slot: [defining] ➔ "The metrics that the team tracked improved significantly."

quests.conceptTitle: Information Snap-In: Preposition + whom/which (Fronted Preposition)
quests.questionSentence: Which sentence incorrectly applies an overly formal structure to an obviously casual context - a text to a close friend?
quests.targetClause: The restaurant to which we went last night was amazing!
quests.completedSentence: Which sentence incorrectly applies an overly formal structure to an obviously casual context - a text to a close friend?
quests.ruleExplanation: A fronted preposition ('to which we went') is a formal, written pattern; it sounds stiff and out of place in a casual text, unlike the other three options.
quests.nativeTip: Look for the version that sounds like a written letter rather than a quick message to a friend.
quests.legoPreview: 🧩 Snap Slot: [defining] ➔ "The restaurant to which we went last night was amazing!"

quests.conceptTitle: Information Snap-In: Omission of Object Relative Pronoun
quests.questionSentence: The feedback from the panel of reviewers ___ we incorporated into the final draft significantly improved the manuscript.
quests.targetClause: (no word needed)
quests.completedSentence: The feedback from the panel of reviewers (no word needed) we incorporated into the final draft significantly improved the manuscript.
quests.ruleExplanation: 'We' is the subject of 'incorporated,' making 'the feedback' - not 'the panel' or 'reviewers' - the object; since it's a thing in a defining clause, the pronoun can be dropped entirely.
quests.nativeTip: 'We' already has a job in this clause - 'incorporated.' Does this defining clause about a thing allow the pronoun to disappear, despite the long descriptive phrase in front of it?
quests.legoPreview: 🧩 Snap Slot: [defining] ➔ "(no word needed)"

quests.conceptTitle: Information Snap-In: Non-Defining Clauses Cannot Omit Their Pronoun
quests.grammarRule: Non-Defining Clauses Cannot Omit Their Pronoun
quests.questionSentence: In her formal resignation letter, she wrote: 'The support from my colleagues, ___ I will always remember fondly, made this decision especially difficult.'
quests.targetClause: which
quests.completedSentence: In her formal resignation letter, she wrote: 'The support from my colleagues, which I will always remember fondly, made this decision especially difficult.'
quests.ruleExplanation: The commas signal a non-defining clause about 'the support,' a thing; 'which' is required, since 'that' can never follow a comma and the pronoun cannot be dropped here.
quests.nativeTip: Notice the commas already present, and remember which pronouns can never follow one.
quests.legoPreview: 🧩 Snap Slot: [non-defining] ➔ "which"

quests.conceptTitle: Information Snap-In: Defining vs Non-Defining Relative Clause
quests.questionSentence: The clinic where I received treatment for over a decade, whose staff became like family, is closing permanently. How many separate relative clauses does this sentence contain, and what does each describe?
quests.targetClause: Two: 'where I received treatment...' describes the clinic (defining); 'whose staff became like family' describes the clinic again (non-defining).
quests.completedSentence: The clinic where I received treatment for over a decade, whose staff became like family, is closing permanently. How many separate relative clauses does this sentence contain, and what does each describe?
quests.ruleExplanation: There are two relative clauses: 'where I received treatment for over a decade' (defining, no commas, describing the clinic) and 'whose staff became like family' (non-defining, set off by commas, also describing the clinic).
quests.nativeTip: Work through the sentence piece by piece and check the punctuation and pronoun of each clause separately.
quests.legoPreview: 🧩 Snap Slot: [non-defining] ➔ "Two: 'where I received treatment...' describes the clinic (defining); 'whose staff became like family' describes the clinic again (non-defining)."

quests.conceptTitle: Information Snap-In: Reduced Passive Relative Clause
quests.questionSentence: The candidate shortlisted for the position, whom the panel unanimously recommended, starts Monday. Which statement about this sentence is true?
quests.targetClause: 'Shortlisted for the position' is a reduced passive clause; 'whom the panel unanimously recommended' is a full non-defining clause - both correctly describe 'the candidate.'
quests.completedSentence: The candidate shortlisted for the position, whom the panel unanimously recommended, starts Monday. Which statement about this sentence is true?
quests.ruleExplanation: 'Shortlisted for the position' is a reduced passive clause, and 'whom the panel unanimously recommended' is a full non-defining clause - both describe 'the candidate.'
quests.nativeTip: Check each descriptive piece separately: is it a reduced clause or a full one, and what noun does it attach to?
quests.legoPreview: 🧩 Snap Slot: [non-defining] ➔ "'Shortlisted for the position' is a reduced passive clause; 'whom the panel unanimously recommended' is a full non-defining clause - both correctly describe 'the candidate.'"

quests.conceptTitle: Information Snap-In: Preposition + whom/which (Fronted Preposition)
quests.questionSentence: The regulation ___ the company must comply, updated last month, affects all overseas branches.
quests.targetClause: with which
quests.completedSentence: The regulation with which the company must comply, updated last month, affects all overseas branches.
quests.ruleExplanation: 'Comply with' needs its preposition; in the formal, fronted pattern it moves in front of 'which': 'with which the company must comply.'
quests.nativeTip: Say the phrase as a normal sentence first: 'the company must comply ___ the regulation.' Which preposition belongs there, and where does it sit in the formal pattern?
quests.legoPreview: 🧩 Snap Slot: [defining] ➔ "with which"

quests.conceptTitle: Information Snap-In: That Cannot Introduce Non-Defining Clauses
quests.questionSentence: Fix this sentence: 'The vaccine, developed over three years, that received emergency approval last week, is now being distributed nationwide.'
quests.targetClause: The vaccine, developed over three years, which received emergency approval last week, is now being distributed nationwide.
quests.completedSentence: Fix this sentence: 'The vaccine, developed over three years, that received emergency approval last week, is now being distributed nationwide.'
quests.ruleExplanation: 'That' cannot follow a comma; since the vaccine is already uniquely identified, this second clause is non-defining and needs 'which' instead.
quests.nativeTip: One relative pronoun here is not allowed to follow a comma - find it and replace it.
quests.legoPreview: 🧩 Snap Slot: [non-defining] ➔ "The vaccine, developed over three years, which received emergency approval last week, is now being distributed nationwide."

quests.conceptTitle: Information Snap-In: Quantifier + of + whom/which
quests.questionSentence: Which sentence has no errors at all?
quests.targetClause: The interns, most of whom had no prior experience, quickly became valuable team members.
quests.completedSentence: Which sentence has no errors at all?
quests.ruleExplanation: 'Most of whom' is the correct pattern for people after a preposition, and both commas correctly frame this non-defining clause about the interns.
quests.nativeTip: Check the pronoun after 'of' and both commas around the non-defining clause.
quests.legoPreview: 🧩 Snap Slot: [non-defining] ➔ "The interns, most of whom had no prior experience, quickly became valuable team members."

quests.conceptTitle: Information Snap-In: Defining vs Non-Defining Relative Clause
quests.questionSentence: Which of these four sentences has no grammatical errors?
quests.targetClause: The clinic where I was treated, whose staff I still keep in touch with, closed last year.
quests.completedSentence: Which of these four sentences has no grammatical errors?
quests.ruleExplanation: 'Where I was treated' correctly identifies the clinic without commas... actually here it is non-defining since the clinic is unique, and 'whose staff I still keep in touch with' correctly shows possession, both properly punctuated.
quests.nativeTip: Check each clause's punctuation and pronoun choice separately - one shows place, the other shows possession.
quests.legoPreview: 🧩 Snap Slot: [non-defining] ➔ "The clinic where I was treated, whose staff I still keep in touch with, closed last year."

quests.conceptTitle: Information Snap-In: Preposition + whom/which (Fronted Preposition)
quests.questionSentence: Out of these four options, which one is fully correct?
quests.targetClause: The proposal for which the board voted unanimously, submitted just before the deadline, will be reviewed again next quarter.
quests.completedSentence: Out of these four options, which one is fully correct?
quests.ruleExplanation: 'For which the board voted unanimously' correctly follows a preposition with 'which,' and 'submitted just before the deadline' is a correctly punctuated non-defining reduced clause.
quests.nativeTip: Check the pronoun after the preposition, the voice of the participle, and whether commas are present where the clause is non-defining.
quests.legoPreview: 🧩 Snap Slot: [non-defining] ➔ "The proposal for which the board voted unanimously, submitted just before the deadline, will be reviewed again next quarter."

quests.conceptTitle: Information Snap-In: Antecedent Identification
quests.questionSentence: The negotiator whose calm demeanor defused the crisis, praised widely in the press, declined all interview requests. What is the antecedent of 'praised widely in the press'?
quests.targetClause: the negotiator
quests.completedSentence: The negotiator whose calm demeanor defused the crisis, praised widely in the press, declined all interview requests. What is the antecedent of 'praised widely in the press'?
quests.ruleExplanation: 'The negotiator' - not the demeanor, the crisis, or the interview requests - is who was praised widely in the press; this is a second, non-defining detail about the negotiator already identified by the 'whose' clause.
quests.nativeTip: Work backward - who was actually praised in the press coverage of this story?
quests.legoPreview: 🧩 Snap Slot: [non-defining] ➔ "the negotiator"

quests.conceptTitle: Information Snap-In: Omission of Object Relative Pronoun
quests.questionSentence: The estimate ___ the contractor initially provided, revised twice since then, still seems optimistic.
quests.targetClause: (no word needed)
quests.completedSentence: The estimate (no word needed) the contractor initially provided, revised twice since then, still seems optimistic.
quests.ruleExplanation: 'The contractor' is the subject of 'provided,' making 'the estimate' the object; since it's a thing in a defining clause, the pronoun can be dropped entirely.
quests.nativeTip: 'The contractor' already has a job in this clause - 'provided.' Does this defining clause about a thing allow the pronoun to disappear?
quests.legoPreview: 🧩 Snap Slot: [defining] ➔ "(no word needed)"

quests.conceptTitle: Information Snap-In: Omission of Object Relative Pronoun
quests.questionSentence: Which sentence is best suited for a formal client-facing project update?
quests.targetClause: The milestones that were originally scheduled for March, delayed due to supply issues, have now been met.
quests.completedSentence: Which sentence is best suited for a formal client-facing project update?
quests.ruleExplanation: This version keeps the full pronoun, matches the formal register expected in a client update, and correctly punctuates the non-defining reduced clause describing the milestones.
quests.nativeTip: Check register, punctuation, and subject-verb agreement all at once.
quests.legoPreview: 🧩 Snap Slot: [non-defining] ➔ "The milestones that were originally scheduled for March, delayed due to supply issues, have now been met."

quests.conceptTitle: Information Snap-In: Defining vs Non-Defining Relative Clause
quests.questionSentence: The report submitted by the consultant, whose findings the board initially disputed, was ultimately the same document that convinced them to change course. Identify every relative structure in this sentence and what each one describes.
quests.targetClause: 'submitted by the consultant' (reduced, describes 'the report'); 'whose findings the board initially disputed' (non-defining, describes 'the consultant'); 'that convinced them to change course' (defining, describes 'the same document').
quests.completedSentence: The report submitted by the consultant, whose findings the board initially disputed, was ultimately the same document that convinced them to change course. Identify every relative structure in this sentence and what each one describes.
quests.ruleExplanation: This sentence contains three relative structures: a reduced passive clause describing the report, a non-defining possessive clause describing the consultant, and a final defining clause identifying which document convinced the board - each studied separately across this course, now working together.
quests.nativeTip: Work through the sentence piece by piece: a reduced clause, a non-defining 'whose' clause, and a final defining clause - check what each one actually attaches to.
quests.legoPreview: 🧩 Snap Slot: [non-defining] ➔ "'submitted by the consultant' (reduced, describes 'the report'); 'whose findings the board initially disputed' (non-defining, describes 'the consultant'); 'that convinced them to change course' (defining, describes 'the same document')."

quests.conceptTitle: Information Snap-In: Defining vs Non-Defining Relative Clause
quests.questionSentence: You are writing a formal recommendation letter for a former employee. Which sentence best fits this context?
quests.targetClause: The initiative that she led, which increased department efficiency by twenty percent, remains a benchmark for the team.
quests.completedSentence: You are writing a formal recommendation letter for a former employee. Which sentence best fits this context?
quests.ruleExplanation: 'That she led' is a correctly unpunctuated defining clause identifying the initiative, and 'which increased department efficiency by twenty percent' is a correctly comma-separated non-defining clause adding detail - both fit the formal register.
quests.nativeTip: Check whether each clause needs commas, whether 'that' appears where it shouldn't, and whether any pronoun has been dropped where it must stay.
quests.legoPreview: 🧩 Snap Slot: [non-defining] ➔ "The initiative that she led, which increased department efficiency by twenty percent, remains a benchmark for the team."

quests.conceptTitle: Information Snap-In: Defining vs Non-Defining Relative Clause
quests.questionSentence: Which sentence demonstrates correct, natural use of relative clauses across a defining clause, a non-defining clause, and a reduced clause all in one sentence?
quests.targetClause: The teacher who first inspired my love of writing, now retired and living abroad, still replies to every email I send her.
quests.completedSentence: Which sentence demonstrates correct, natural use of relative clauses across a defining clause, a non-defining clause, and a reduced clause all in one sentence?
quests.ruleExplanation: This option correctly combines all three structures studied throughout the course: a defining clause needing no comma, a non-defining reduced clause properly set off by commas, and accurate pronoun and participle choices throughout - a fitting close to everything this curriculum has taught.
quests.nativeTip: This is the final question of the course - check every skill at once: pronoun role, defining versus non-defining punctuation, and whether the reduced clause uses the correct participle.
quests.legoPreview: 🧩 Snap Slot: [non-defining] ➔ "The teacher who first inspired my love of writing, now retired and living abroad, still replies to every email I send her."
